# Orchestrating ML pipelines {#sec-ch-ops-orch}

> *"Workflows are defined as code, so that they become more maintainable,
> versionable, testable, and collaborative."* — Apache Airflow documentation
> [@airflow2026]



::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain what an **orchestrator** adds to a scheduler like cron —
  dependencies, retries, backfills, parameters, observability — and compare
  the main tools;
- represent a pipeline as a **DAG**, compute a topological order with
  **Kahn's algorithm** (proved correct, cycles detected), and bound the
  running time with $W$ workers between $\max(\text{work}/W, \text{span})$ and
  $\text{work}/W + \text{span}$;
- write **Airflow** DAGs with the TaskFlow API, pass **returned values**
  between tasks through XCom (and know what not to pass), schedule them over
  data intervals, and run them locally with `airflow dags test`;
- make tasks **idempotent** with partitioned, atomically written outputs, and
  prove that retries and backfills then leave the same final state as a
  single clean run;
- decide **when to retrain**: the optimal retraining period under a linear
  decay (a square-root law), drift-triggered retraining with CUSUM, and the
  **feedback loops** that a careless retraining pipeline creates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
What an orchestrator is; setting up an environment for orchestration; Apache
Airflow; writing a DAG; passing values returned by one task to the next.
:::

## What an orchestrator does {#sec-ops-orchestrator}

### Beyond cron

The simplest way to run a pipeline every night is a **cron** entry: at 02:17,
run `pipeline.sh`. It breaks as soon as the pipeline has more than one step:
if the third of five steps fails, cron does not know, cannot retry just that
step, cannot run the remaining steps when it is fixed, cannot re-run last
Tuesday for a corrected input, and cannot show what ran when. An
**orchestrator** is a scheduler that knows the **structure** of the work
[@airflow2026]:

- **dependencies**: tasks form a DAG; a task starts when its upstream tasks
  have succeeded;
- **retries** with delays per task, timeouts, and alerts on failure;
- **parameters**: each run is tied to a **data interval** (e.g. the day it
  processes), so that re-running a past interval — a **backfill** — processes
  that interval's data, not today's;
- **state and observability**: which task of which run succeeded, failed or
  is waiting; logs per attempt; durations over time;
- **concurrency** limits and pools, so that a backfill of 100 days does not
  saturate a database.

The main open-source orchestrators differ in emphasis: **Apache Airflow**
(Python DAG files, a scheduler with a metadata database; the most widely
deployed), **Prefect** and **Dagster** (Python-native, with Dagster centred on
the *assets* the pipeline produces), **Kubeflow Pipelines** and **Argo
Workflows** (each task a container on Kubernetes, Part V). This chapter uses
Airflow; the ideas transfer.

### DAGs and topological order

A pipeline is a directed graph whose vertices are tasks and whose edges $u \to
v$ mean "$v$ needs $u$". It can be executed only if there is an order in
which every task comes after all its upstream tasks — a **topological
order** — which exists exactly when the graph has no cycle.

::: {#thm-ops-kahn}
## Kahn's algorithm
Repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edges, appending it to a list,
and delete its outgoing edges. (i) If the graph is acyclic, the procedure
removes every vertex and the list is a topological order. (ii) If it stops
with vertices left, the remaining graph contains a cycle. It runs in $O(V +
E)$ time [@kahn1962].
:::

*In one line:* an acyclic graph always has a task with no pending
dependencies; removing it leaves an acyclic graph — so the process never gets
stuck unless there is a cycle.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ops-kahn
**Every non-empty acyclic graph has a vertex with no incoming edge.** Start
anywhere and walk *backwards* along incoming edges; if every vertex had an
incoming edge the walk could continue for ever, and since the graph is finite
it would revisit a vertex — a cycle. (i) Removing a vertex and its edges
keeps the graph acyclic, so by induction on the number of vertices Kahn's
procedure removes all of them. When a vertex $v$ is appended, it has no
incoming edges left, so all its upstream vertices were removed — appended —
before it: the list is a topological order. (ii) If the procedure stops with
a non-empty remainder, every remaining vertex has an incoming edge from
another remaining vertex; by the backward walk above, the remainder contains a
cycle. Complexity: each vertex enters the queue once and each edge decrements
an in-degree once. $\blacksquare$
:::

With $W$ workers, how long does a DAG take? Let the **work** $T_1 = \sum_v
w_v$ be the total running time of the tasks and the **span** $T_\infty$ the
weight of the critical path (@prp-ops-critical-path).

::: {#prp-ops-greedy}
## Bounds on the makespan with $W$ workers
Any schedule on $W$ workers takes at least $\max(T_1/W, T_\infty)$. A
**greedy** schedule — whenever a worker is idle and a task is ready, start it
— takes at most $T_1/W + T_\infty$, hence within a factor 2 of optimal
[@graham1969; @brent1974].
:::

*In one line:* at every moment a greedy scheduler either keeps all workers
busy (that time is at most $T_1/W$ in total) or is running every ready task,
which shortens the remaining critical path.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-greedy
Lower bound: $W$ workers do at most $W$ units of work per unit time, and the
tasks of a path must run one after the other. Upper bound: split the greedy
schedule's time into **full** intervals (all $W$ workers busy) and **non-full**
ones. Full intervals do $W$ units of work per unit of time, so they last at
most $T_1/W$ in total. During a non-full interval every ready task is running
(otherwise an idle worker would start it). Follow, backwards from the task
that finishes last, a chain of tasks each of which was the last-finishing
predecessor of the next: whenever no task of the chain is running, all
predecessors of the next chain task have finished, so that task is ready, so
it is running unless all workers are busy. Hence every non-full instant is
spent running some task of the chain, and the non-full intervals last at most
the chain's weight, at most $T_\infty$. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#5e31a955 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def kahn(tasks: dict[str, list[str]]) -> list[str]:
    """tasks: name -> upstream names. Returns a topological order or raises on a cycle."""
    indeg = {t: len(up) for t, up in tasks.items()}
    down = {t: [] for t in tasks}
    for t, up in tasks.items():
        for u in up:
            down[u].append(t)
    ready = deque(sorted(t for t, d in indeg.items() if d == 0))
    order = []
    while ready:
        t = ready.popleft()
        order.append(t)
        for v in down[t]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                ready.append(v)
    if len(order) < len(tasks):
        raise ValueError(f"cycle among {sorted(set(tasks) - set(order))}")
    return order

pipeline = {"ingest": [], "validate": ["ingest"], "features": ["validate"], "predict": ["features"],
            "monitor": ["predict"], "train": ["features"], "evaluate": ["train"], "gate": ["evaluate", "monitor"],
            "report": ["gate"]}
print(" -> ".join(kahn(pipeline)))
try:
    kahn({**pipeline, "ingest": ["report"]})          # a loop back to the start
except ValueError as e:
    print("rejected:", e)
```

```
ingest -> validate -> features -> predict -> train -> monitor -> evaluate -> gate -> report
rejected: cycle among ['evaluate', 'features', 'gate', 'ingest', 'monitor', 'predict', 'report', 'train', 'validate']
```
:::
:::


### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops8-dag-easy}
## Easy — orders and cycles by hand
Tasks: `a` (no upstream), `b` needs `a`, `c` needs `a`, `d` needs `b` and `c`,
`e` needs `c`, `f` needs `d` and `e`. (a) Give two different topological
orders. (b) With durations a 1, b 3, c 2, d 1, e 4, f 1 and two workers, compute
work, span and the bounds of @prp-ops-greedy. (c) Add "`a` needs `f`": where
does Kahn's algorithm stop?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The span is the heaviest path from `a` to `f`. In (c), no task has in-degree
zero at the start.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#04dae102 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
small = {"a": [], "b": ["a"], "c": ["a"], "d": ["b", "c"], "e": ["c"], "f": ["d", "e"]}
w = {"a": 1, "b": 3, "c": 2, "d": 1, "e": 4, "f": 1}
print("one order:", kahn(small))
finish = {}
for t in kahn(small):
    finish[t] = w[t] + max((finish[u] for u in small[t]), default=0)
T1, Tinf, W = sum(w.values()), max(finish.values()), 2
print(f"work {T1}, span {Tinf}: any schedule >= {max(T1 / W, Tinf)}, greedy <= {T1 / W + Tinf}")
try:
    kahn({**small, "a": ["f"]})
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
one order: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']
work 12, span 8: any schedule >= 8, greedy <= 14.0
cycle among ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']
```
:::
:::


(a) `a, b, c, d, e, f` and `a, c, e, b, d, f` are both valid. (b) Work 12,
span 8 (a → c → e → f): any two-worker schedule needs at least 8, a greedy
one at most 14 — here greedy achieves 8. (c) With `a` needing `f` there is a
cycle a → c → e → f → a and every task has a pending dependency: Kahn's
algorithm removes nothing and reports all six.
:::

::: {#exr-ops8-dag-medium}
## Medium — a greedy scheduler, measured
Simulate a greedy scheduler with $W$ workers (an event queue of finishing
times) on 200 random DAGs of 30 tasks (each task depends on each earlier one
with probability 0.1; durations uniform in $[1, 10]$). For $W = 1, 2, 4, 8$
report how close the makespan is to the lower bound $\max(T_1/W, T_\infty)$,
and check that it never exceeds $T_1/W + T_\infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Keep a heap of (finish time, task) for running tasks; when one finishes,
decrement its successors' in-degrees and start ready tasks on the free
workers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#617c1082 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def greedy_makespan(up, w, W):
    down = {t: [] for t in up}
    indeg = {t: len(u) for t, u in up.items()}
    for t, us in up.items():
        for u in us:
            down[u].append(t)
    ready = [t for t in up if indeg[t] == 0]
    running, now = [], 0.0
    while ready or running:
        while ready and len(running) < W:
            t = ready.pop(0)
            heapq.heappush(running, (now + w[t], t))
        now, t = heapq.heappop(running)
        for v in down[t]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                ready.append(v)
    return now

rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
for W in (1, 2, 4, 8):
    ratios, violations = [], 0
    for _ in range(200):
        n = 30
        up = {i: [j for j in range(i) if rng.random() < 0.1] for i in range(n)}
        w = {i: float(rng.uniform(1, 10)) for i in range(n)}
        fin = {}
        for i in range(n):
            fin[i] = w[i] + max((fin[j] for j in up[i]), default=0)
        T1, Tinf = sum(w.values()), max(fin.values())
        m = greedy_makespan(up, w, W)
        ratios.append(m / max(T1 / W, Tinf))
        violations += m > T1 / W + Tinf + 1e-9
    print(f"W = {W}: makespan / lower bound: mean {np.mean(ratios):.3f}, max {np.max(ratios):.3f}; "
          f"upper bound violated {violations} times")
```

```

W = 2: makespan / lower bound: mean 1.037, max 1.159; upper bound violated 0 times
W = 4: makespan / lower bound: mean 1.150, max 1.419; upper bound violated 0 times
W = 8: makespan / lower bound: mean 1.023, max 1.262; upper bound violated 0 times
```
:::
:::


With one worker the makespan is exactly the work; with more workers the
greedy schedule stays within about 15 % of the lower bound on average and
never violates the upper bound, as @prp-ops-greedy guarantees. Beyond the
point where the span dominates, extra workers help nothing — the shape of the
DAG, not the cluster size, limits the pipeline.
:::

::: {#exr-ops8-dag-hard}
## Hard — a tiny orchestrator
Write a small orchestrator: tasks are Python functions with upstream
dependencies and a retry policy (maximum attempts, exponential backoff); they
run on a pool of $W$ threads as soon as their dependencies have succeeded; a
task that exhausts its retries marks all its downstream tasks as
**upstream failed** without running them. Test it on the pipeline of this
section with a task that fails twice before succeeding and another that
always fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
A `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` and a loop that waits for the first
finished future (`wait(..., return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)`) are enough. Keep a
state per task: pending, running, success, failed, upstream_failed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#1a6e03ab .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, wait, FIRST_COMPLETED

def orchestrate(tasks, upstream, W=3, max_tries=3, base_delay=0.01):
    state = {t: "pending" for t in tasks}
    tries = {t: 0 for t in tasks}
    log = []
    def attempt(t):
        tries[t] += 1
        if tries[t] > 1:
            time.sleep(base_delay * 2 ** (tries[t] - 2))      # backoff before a retry
        tasks[t]()
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(W) as pool:
        running = {}
        while True:
            for t in tasks:                                     # start every ready task
                if state[t] == "pending" and all(state[u] == "success" for u in upstream[t]) \
                        and len(running) < W:
                    state[t] = "running"
                    running[pool.submit(attempt, t)] = t
                if state[t] == "pending" and any(state[u] in ("failed", "upstream_failed") for u in upstream[t]):
                    state[t] = "upstream_failed"
            if not running:
                break
            done, _ = wait(running, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)
            for f in done:
                t = running.pop(f)
                if f.exception() is None:
                    state[t] = "success"
                elif tries[t] < max_tries:
                    log.append(f"{t}: attempt {tries[t]} failed, retrying")
                    running[pool.submit(attempt, t)] = t
                else:
                    state[t] = "failed"
                    log.append(f"{t}: failed after {tries[t]} attempts")
    return state, log

flaky_calls = {"n": 0}
def flaky():
    flaky_calls["n"] += 1
    if flaky_calls["n"] <= 2:
        raise ConnectionError("source not reachable")
def broken():
    raise ValueError("schema mismatch")
ok = lambda: time.sleep(0.01)
tasks = {t: ok for t in pipeline}
tasks["ingest"], tasks["train"] = flaky, broken
state, log = orchestrate(tasks, pipeline)
print("\n".join(log))
print(json.dumps(state, indent=1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
ingest: attempt 1 failed, retrying
ingest: attempt 2 failed, retrying
train: attempt 1 failed, retrying
train: attempt 2 failed, retrying
train: failed after 3 attempts
{
 "ingest": "success",
 "validate": "success",
 "features": "success",
 "predict": "success",
 "monitor": "success",
 "train": "failed",
 "evaluate": "upstream_failed",
 "gate": "upstream_failed",
 "report": "upstream_failed"
}
```
:::
:::


`ingest` succeeds on its third attempt and the branch through `predict` and
`monitor` runs; `train` fails three times, so `evaluate`, `gate` and `report`
are never run but marked as **upstream failed** — distinct from failing, so
that an operator knows where to look. Real orchestrators add what this one
lacks: persistent state (to survive a crash of the orchestrator itself),
per-run parameters, logs per attempt, and a UI.
:::

## Airflow: DAGs, tasks and returned values {#sec-ops-airflow}

### The pieces

In Airflow a **DAG** is defined in a Python file placed in the *DAGs folder*.
The **scheduler** parses the files, creates a **DAG run** for each scheduled
**data interval**, and hands **task instances** to an **executor**; their
states, and the small values they exchange, live in a **metadata database**
[@airflow2026]. With the **TaskFlow API**, a task is a decorated Python
function, and calling one task with the result of another *declares* both the
dependency and the data passed:

- `@dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=..., catchup=False)` defines the DAG;
  `catchup=True` would create runs for every past interval since the start
  date (a backfill);
- `@task(retries=2, retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=5))` defines a task with its
  retry policy;
- the **return value** of a task is stored as an **XCom** ("cross-
  communication") — serialised (JSON by default) into the metadata database —
  and passed to the downstream task that receives it as an argument;
- context values such as `ds` (the logical date, `YYYY-MM-DD`) are injected
  into tasks that ask for them.

XComs are meant for **small** values: a path, a hash, a few metrics. Data go
to storage (files, object stores, tables), and the XCom carries the
reference — otherwise the metadata database fills with data frames and every
task pays to serialise them.

### A scoring DAG

A daily DAG that scores the posts of its day with the local model: `ingest`
writes the day's posts to a partition and returns its path and hash; `score`
writes predictions next to it and returns a summary; `report` checks the
summary against the reference class mix. Each task writes **only its
partition**, atomically:


**`dags/score_posts.py`**

``` {.python}
"""Daily scoring of the posts of each data interval with the local sentiment model."""
import hashlib
import json
import os
import sys
from datetime import timedelta
from pathlib import Path

import pendulum
from airflow.sdk import dag, task

sys.path.insert(0, os.environ["OPSBOOK_DIR"])        # opsbook: the synthetic post source
DATA = Path(os.environ.get("PIPELINE_DATA", "data"))
MODEL = Path(os.environ.get("PIPELINE_MODEL", "model.joblib"))
REFERENCE = {"negative": 0.30, "neutral": 0.40, "positive": 0.30}


def atomic_write(path: Path, text: str) -> None:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp = path.with_suffix(path.suffix + ".tmp")
    tmp.write_text(text)
    tmp.replace(path)                                  # all or nothing


@dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 11, 1, tz="UTC"), catchup=False,
     default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(seconds=1)}, tags=["sentiment"])
def score_posts():
    @task
    def ingest(ds=None) -> dict:
        import opsbook as ob

        day = pendulum.parse(ds)
        posts = ob.make_posts(500, seed=int(day.format("YYYYMMDD")))   # the day's posts
        path = DATA / ds / "posts.csv"
        atomic_write(path, posts.to_csv(index=False))
        return {"path": str(path), "sha256": hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:16],
                "rows": len(posts)}

    @task
    def score(batch: dict) -> dict:
        import joblib
        import pandas as pd

        posts = pd.read_csv(batch["path"])
        model = joblib.load(MODEL)
        labels = ["negative", "neutral", "positive"]
        posts["prediction"] = [labels[i] for i in model.predict(posts["text"])]
        out = Path(batch["path"]).with_name("predictions.csv")
        atomic_write(out, posts.to_csv(index=False))
        shares = posts["prediction"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(4).to_dict()
        return {"path": str(out), "shares": shares, "input_sha256": batch["sha256"]}

    @task
    def report(summary: dict, ds=None) -> dict:
        gap = max(abs(summary["shares"].get(k, 0) - v) for k, v in REFERENCE.items())
        result = {"date": ds, "max_share_gap": round(gap, 4), "alert": gap > 0.08}
        atomic_write(DATA / ds / "report.json", json.dumps(result))
        return result

    report(score(ingest()))


score_posts()
```



`airflow dags test` runs one DAG run in a single process, without a scheduler
— the way to try a DAG locally. Airflow lives in its own virtual environment
(it pins hundreds of dependencies through a constraints file), which must also
contain what the tasks import — here scikit-learn, pandas and joblib, installed
under the same constraints; its home directory, with a SQLite metadata
database, is a temporary folder:

``` {.python .cell-code}
AF_ENV = {"AIRFLOW_HOME": str(af), "AIRFLOW__CORE__DAGS_FOLDER": str(af / "dags"),
          "AIRFLOW__CORE__LOAD_EXAMPLES": "False", "PIPELINE_DATA": str(af / "data"),
          "PIPELINE_MODEL": str(af / "model.joblib"), "PYTHONWARNINGS": "ignore",
          "OPSBOOK_DIR": str(Path.cwd())}
airflow = str(Path(ob.venv_python("airflow")).parent / "airflow")
ob.run(f"{airflow} db migrate", env=AF_ENV, check=True, timeout=600)

def dags_test(dag_id, date):
    p = ob.run(f"{airflow} dags test {dag_id} {date}", env=AF_ENV, timeout=600)
    out = p.stdout + p.stderr
    tasks = re.findall(r"\[DAG TEST\] starting task_id=(\w+)", out)
    returned = re.findall(r"Returned value was: (.*?) \[airflow", out)
    state = re.search(r"DagRun Finished: .*?state=(\w+)", out)
    return tasks, returned, state.group(1) if state else "unknown"

tasks, returned, state = dags_test("score_posts", "2026-11-17")
for t, r in zip(tasks, returned):
    print(f"{t:7s} returned {ob.mask(r)}")
print("DAG run:", state)
print(sorted(p.name for p in (af / "data" / "2026-11-17").iterdir()))
```

Each task's return value went through the metadata database to the next
task: small dictionaries with paths, a hash and the class shares — never the
posts themselves. The partition `data/2026-11-17/` holds the day's three
files.

### Idempotent tasks and safe backfills

Retries and backfills run tasks **again**. They are harmless only if running
a task twice has the same effect as running it once — idempotence again
(@def-api-idempotent), now at the level of a pipeline.

::: {#prp-ops-backfill}
## Partitioned, deterministic tasks make re-runs safe
Suppose each task (i) writes only the outputs of its own data interval
(its **partition**), replacing them atomically, and (ii) computes them
deterministically from its inputs (which are earlier partitions or fixed
artefacts). Then any sequence of runs, retries and backfills in which every
task of every interval eventually succeeds, in an order compatible with the
DAG, leaves the storage in the same state as one clean run of every interval.
:::

*In one line:* each partition ends up as the deterministic function of its
inputs, no matter how many times it was written or what partial attempts
preceded it.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-backfill
Consider the partition $P_{v,d}$ written by task $v$ for interval $d$. By
(i), only attempts of $(v, d)$ write it, and atomically, so its final content
is that of the **last successful** attempt (a failed attempt leaves the
previous content, never a half-written one). By (ii) that content is
$f_v(\text{inputs})$, and the inputs are partitions of upstream tasks (or
fixed artefacts). The order is compatible with the DAG, so when the last
successful attempt of $(v, d)$ ran, its upstream partitions had already reached
their final content — by induction along a topological order — and they do
not change afterwards (a later re-run of an upstream task rewrites the same
content, by the same argument). Hence every partition equals what one clean
run produces. $\blacksquare$
:::

The hypotheses are exactly the habits that break pipelines when missing: a
task that **appends** to a shared file (not partitioned), one that reads
"today" from the clock instead of its data interval (not deterministic in its
inputs), one that writes in place (not atomic). The tasks above read `ds`,
write `data/<ds>/` and replace files atomically (@sec-atomic-writes).

::: {#exr-ops8-airflow-easy}
## Easy — what goes through XCom?
For the DAG above: (a) which values are stored in the metadata database for
one run, and roughly how large are they? (b) A colleague changes `ingest` to
return the posts themselves (`posts.to_dict()`): what changes, and why is it a
bad idea at 500 000 posts per day? (c) What would happen to a backfill if
`ingest` used `pendulum.now()` instead of `ds`?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Every returned value is serialised and written to the database; a backfill
runs past intervals *now*.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Three small JSON documents — `ingest`'s path, hash and row count, `score`'s
path, shares and input hash, `report`'s verdict — a few hundred bytes each.
(b) The XCom would hold the whole table: hundreds of megabytes serialised to
JSON into the metadata database at 500 000 posts, deserialised again by the
next task, slowing the scheduler for every DAG (and many deployments limit
XCom sizes). Data go to storage; XComs carry references. (c) Every backfilled
run would process *today's* posts and write them into the partition of a past
day: the backfill would silently produce wrong history, and two runs for
different days would contain the same data — @prp-ops-backfill's hypothesis
(ii) is violated.
:::

``` {.python .cell-code}
def patch(src, old, new):
    """Replace a fragment of the DAG file (whose task bodies are indented by 8 spaces), or fail."""
    old, new = textwrap.dedent(old).strip("\n"), textwrap.dedent(new).strip("\n")
    lines = [l for l in src.splitlines() if l.strip() == old.splitlines()[0].strip()]
    assert lines, f"fragment not found: {old.splitlines()[0]!r}"
    indent = lines[0][: len(lines[0]) - len(lines[0].lstrip())]
    old_i = textwrap.indent(old, indent)
    new_i = textwrap.indent(new, indent, predicate=lambda l: True).replace(indent + "\n", "\n")
    assert old_i in src, "fragment not found with its indentation"
    return src.replace(old_i, new_i)

dag_src = (af / "dags" / "score_posts.py").read_text()
dag_src = patch(dag_src, '''posts = ob.make_posts(500, seed=int(day.format("YYYYMMDD")))   # the day's posts''', '''
    shifted = ds in os.environ.get("NEGATIVE_DAYS", "").split(",")
    prior = (0.6, 0.2, 0.2) if shifted else (0.3, 0.4, 0.3)
    posts = ob.make_posts(500, seed=int(day.format("YYYYMMDD")), prior=prior)''')
dag_src = patch(dag_src, "report(score(ingest()))", '''
    @task.branch
    def decide(result: dict) -> str:
        return "notify" if result["alert"] else "done"

    @task
    def notify(ds=None):
        atomic_write(DATA / ds / "alert.txt", "class mix far from the reference\\n")

    @task
    def done():
        pass

    decide(report(score(ingest()))) >> [notify(), done()]''')
(af / "dags" / "score_posts.py").write_text(dag_src)
AF_ENV["NEGATIVE_DAYS"] = "2026-11-12"
for day in ("2026-11-11", "2026-11-12"):
    tasks, returned, state = dags_test("score_posts", day)
    files = sorted(p.name for p in (af / "data" / day).iterdir())
    print(f"{day}: ran {tasks} -> {state}; files {files}")
```

With partitioned, atomic, deterministic tasks, a failure followed by a retry,
a missing output and a full re-run of five days leave every file

classic way backfills corrupt data.

## When to retrain {#sec-ops-retrain}

### Triggers and their costs

A model is retrained on a **schedule** (every week), on a **trigger** (a drift
or quality monitor fires, @sec-ch-ops-monitor), or when enough **new labels**
have accumulated. Retraining has costs — compute, labelling, validation,
the risk and churn of a release (@prp-ops-churn) — and benefits: the
accuracy lost to drift is regained. A simple model makes the trade-off
explicit.

::: {#prp-ops-retrain-period}
## The square-root law for periodic retraining
Suppose that after each retraining the model's accuracy decays linearly,
$a(t) = a_0 - d\,t$, that each point of lost accuracy costs $L$ per unit of
time, and that each retraining costs $K$. Retraining every $T$ units of time
costs on average
$$
c(T) = \frac{K}{T} + \frac{L\,d\,T}{2}
$$ {#eq-ops-retrain-cost}
per unit of time, minimised by
$$
T^\star = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{L\,d}}, \qquad c(T^\star) = \sqrt{2KLd} .
$$
:::

*In one line:* frequent retraining wastes retraining costs, rare retraining
wastes accuracy; the balance point grows only with the square root of the cost
ratio — the economic order quantity of inventory theory [@harris1913].

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-retrain-period
Over one period the lost accuracy at time $t$ is $dt$, costing $L\,d\,t$ per
unit time; integrated over $[0, T]$ it is $L d T^2/2$. Adding $K$ and dividing
by $T$ gives @eq-ops-retrain-cost. On $T > 0$, $c'(T) = -K/T^2 + Ld/2$
vanishes at $T^\star$, and $c''(T) = 2K/T^3 > 0$, so $T^\star$ is the
minimum; substituting gives $c(T^\star) = K/T^\star + LdT^\star/2 =
2\sqrt{KLd/2} = \sqrt{2KLd}$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Accuracy rarely decays linearly: a model often holds steady and then drops
when the world changes — a new product, a new slang, an event. Then a fixed
schedule retrains too often in quiet times and too late after a change, and a
**trigger** — a change detector such as CUSUM on a monitored quantity — does
better, at the price of false alarms (@exr-ops8-retrain-medium).

### Feedback loops

A retraining pipeline closes a loop: the model's predictions influence which
data are collected and how they are labelled, and those data train the next
model. Sculley et al. call this a **hidden feedback loop**
[@sculley2015, §4]: a moderation model whose flagged posts are the only ones
reviewed and labelled; a recommender trained on clicks on the items it chose
to show; pseudo-labels taken from the model's own confident predictions. The
loop can amplify the model's own errors. The remedies are design decisions,
not algorithms: keep a random **holdout** of the traffic that is labelled
regardless of the model, log what the model decided, and evaluate on data the
model did not select (@exr-ops8-retrain-hard).

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops8-retrain-easy}
## Easy — how often to retrain
A sentiment model loses 0.5 accuracy points per week after each retraining.
Each point of lost accuracy costs 400 € per week in wrong decisions;
retraining (labelling a fresh sample, compute, validation, release) costs
3 000 €. Compute the optimal period, the cost per week at that period, and the
cost per week of retraining every week and every quarter. How does $T^\star$
change if labelling becomes four times cheaper?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$K = 3000$, $L = 400$, $d = 0.5$ points per week; units: weeks and euros.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#089f295d .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
K, L, d = 3000.0, 400.0, 0.5
cost = lambda T: K / T + L * d * T / 2
T_star = np.sqrt(2 * K / (L * d))
print(f"T* = {T_star:.1f} weeks, cost {cost(T_star):.0f} €/week; weekly {cost(1):.0f} €/week; quarterly {cost(13):.0f} €/week")
print(f"labelling 4x cheaper (K = {K / 4:.0f}): T* = {np.sqrt(2 * K / 4 / (L * d)):.1f} weeks")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
T* = 5.5 weeks, cost 1095 €/week; weekly 3100 €/week; quarterly 1531 €/week
labelling 4x cheaper (K = 750): T* = 2.7 weeks
```
:::
:::


Retraining every 5.5 weeks costs about 1 100 € per week; weekly retraining
costs almost three times as much, quarterly retraining about 40 % more. A
retraining four times cheaper halves the optimal period (square root of 4):
cost reductions change *how often*, but much less than proportionally. The
assumption of linear decay is the weak point — the next exercise drops it.
:::

## Medium — scheduled versus triggered
Simulate 104 weeks of a model in production: each week 2 000 posts arrive;
the world changes twice (at weeks 30 and 70, five more positive words flip to
negative each time — a concept shift that lowers accuracy and the share of
predicted negatives). Compare (a) retraining every 8 weeks on the last 4
weeks of labelled posts and (b) retraining when a CUSUM on the weekly share of
predicted negatives fires (then resetting it). Count retrainings and the
average accuracy over the two years.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Generate each week's posts with the `swap` in force that week; "labelled
posts" of the last weeks are those posts with their labels. Use the CUSUM of
@sec-ops-cusum in both directions with a threshold that does not fire in quiet
weeks.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#cell-fig-ops-retrain-policies .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
wave1 = ("cheap", "fast", "smooth", "perfect", "awesome")
wave2 = ("great", "amazing", "happy", "brilliant", "helpful")
def world(week):
    swap = {}
    if week >= 30:
        swap.update({w: 0 for w in wave1})
    if week >= 70:
        swap.update({w: 0 for w in wave2})
    return swap

weeks = [ob.make_posts(2000, seed=3000 + w, swap=world(w)) for w in range(104)]

def simulate(policy):
    model_ = ob.train_model(train.text, train.label)
    ref = np.mean(model_.predict(weeks[0].text) == 0)
    s_up = s_down = 0.0
    accs, retrains = [], 0
    for w in range(104):
        pred = model_.predict(weeks[w].text)
        accs.append(accuracy_score(weeks[w].label, pred))
        share = np.mean(pred == 0)
        s_up, s_down = max(0, s_up + share - ref - 0.01), max(0, s_down - share + ref - 0.01)
        due = (policy == "every 8 weeks" and w % 8 == 7) or (policy == "CUSUM" and max(s_up, s_down) > 0.06)
        if due and w >= 3:
            recent = pd.concat(weeks[w - 3: w + 1])
            model_ = ob.train_model(recent.text, recent.label)
            ref = np.mean(model_.predict(weeks[w].text) == 0)
            s_up = s_down = 0.0
            retrains += 1
    return np.array(accs), retrains

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, policy in enumerate(("every 8 weeks", "CUSUM")):
    accs, n = simulate(policy)
    ax.plot(accs, color=ob.COLORS[i], label=f"{policy}: {n} retrainings, mean accuracy {accs.mean():.3f}")
    print(f"{policy:14s} retrainings {n:2d}, mean accuracy {accs.mean():.4f}, worst week {accs.min():.3f}")
ax.axvline(30, color="#c8c7c2"); ax.axvline(70, color="#c8c7c2")
ax.set_xlabel("week"); ax.set_ylabel("weekly accuracy"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

## Hard — a feedback loop and its fix
A moderation team reviews only the posts that the model predicts as
**negative**. Compare three ways of turning a month of traffic into training
data for the monthly retraining: (a) reviewed posts get their true label and
**unreviewed posts keep the model's own label** ("nobody complained, so the
label is right"); (b) only reviewed posts are used; (c) as (b), plus a **random
holdout** of 10 % of all posts reviewed regardless of the prediction. Start
from a model trained on 1 500 posts, use 3 000 posts per month for ten
months, and let the world change at month 3: eight positive words become
negative (a concept shift). Track the accuracy on fresh, unselected posts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
After the change, posts containing the flipped words are negative but are
predicted positive: who ever corrects that prediction in each pipeline?
Evaluate every month on a fresh sample from the same month's world.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#e0eabae5 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
wave = ("cheap", "fast", "smooth", "perfect", "awesome", "great", "amazing", "happy")
world_m = lambda m: {w: 0 for w in wave} if m >= 2 else {}

def moderation(mode, holdout=0.10, months=10):
    rng_ = np.random.default_rng(0)
    pool = [ob.make_posts(1500, seed=4000)]
    model_ = ob.train_model(pool[0].text, pool[0].label)
    accs = []
    for m in range(months):
        month = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=4100 + m, swap=world_m(m)).reset_index(drop=True)
        pred = model_.predict(month.text)
        flagged = pred == 0
        if mode == "self-labelled":                       # (a) unreviewed posts keep the model's label
            pool.append(month.assign(label=np.where(flagged, month.label, pred)))
        elif mode == "flagged only":                      # (b) only what the model selected
            pool.append(month[flagged])
        else:                                             # (c) plus a random holdout
            pool.append(month[flagged | (rng_.random(len(month)) < holdout)])
        data = pd.concat(pool)
        model_ = ob.train_model(data.text, data.label)
        test_ = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=4200 + m, swap=world_m(m))
        accs.append(accuracy_score(test_.label, model_.predict(test_.text)))
    return accs

table = pd.DataFrame({mode: moderation(mode) for mode in ("self-labelled", "flagged only", "with 10 % holdout")},
                     index=pd.RangeIndex(1, 11, name="month")).round(3)
print(table.T.to_string())
```

Before the change the three pipelines are similar. After it, the
**self-labelled** pipeline is stuck: posts that became negative are predicted
positive, nobody reviews them, and they enter the training data *with the
model's wrong label* — every retraining confirms the error, and the accuracy
stays several points down for good. Training only on reviewed posts avoids
feeding the model its own mistakes, and it recovers — slowly, because it
learns the new meaning only from the few posts that were flagged anyway. The
random holdout recovers fastest: a tenth of the traffic is reviewed whatever
the model says, so the new negatives reach the training data at their true
rate, and the same holdout gives the only unbiased estimate of the model's
accuracy in production. The price is 10 % more reviews — the cost of knowing
what the model misses.
:::

**In the project.** The project asks for an Airflow DAG describing the

paths, hashes and metrics rather than data (@sec-ops-airflow), a **branch**
that decides whether to retrain (@exr-ops8-airflow-medium), a decision based
on a monitor with known false-alarm behaviour rather than on a fixed date
(@exr-ops8-retrain-medium), and a promotion gate after retraining
(@sec-ops-cd). Test the DAG with `airflow dags test` on a few dates and on a
re-run, and write down how labels would reach it without creating a feedback
loop (@exr-ops8-retrain-hard).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Cron for multi-step pipelines**: no dependencies, no retries, no
  backfills.
- **Tasks that read the clock** instead of their data interval; tasks that
  append instead of replacing their partition.
- **Data in XComs**: pass references.
- **Retries on non-idempotent tasks**: duplicates (@prp-ops-backfill).
- **Retraining on a calendar only**: too often in quiet times, too late after
  a change.
- **Training only on what the model selected**: feedback loops; keep a random
  holdout.
:::

## Summary

- Orchestrators run DAGs of tasks with dependencies, retries, data intervals,
  backfills and state. Kahn's algorithm orders a DAG in $O(V + E)$ and detects
  cycles; with $W$ workers the makespan lies between $\max(T_1/W, T_\infty)$
  and $T_1/W + T_\infty$ for a greedy scheduler.
- Airflow: DAG files, scheduler, executor, metadata database; TaskFlow tasks
  whose returned values travel as XComs (small values only); branches;
  `airflow dags test` for local runs.
- Partitioned, atomic, deterministic tasks make retries and backfills
  converge to the state of one clean run.
- Periodic retraining under linear decay has the optimal period $T^\star =
  \sqrt{2K/(Ld)}$; under sudden changes a drift trigger retrains when it
  matters. Retraining on data the model selected creates feedback loops; a
  random holdout breaks them.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ops8-pools}
**A backfill that does not overload.** A backfill of 90 days must run a
`score` task that queries a database allowing at most 3 concurrent
connections, while `ingest` tasks are free. With 10 workers, each `ingest`
taking 1 minute and each `score` 4 minutes, compute the makespan with and
without a pool of size 3 for `score` (greedy scheduling), and explain why the
pool is still necessary.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#5bbdcd30 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def makespan_with_pool(n_days, W, pool):
    # events: (time, kind, day); greedy: start ingests and scores whenever workers (and pool slots) allow
    now, running, ready_ingest, ready_score = 0.0, [], list(range(n_days)), []
    busy_pool = 0
    while ready_ingest or ready_score or running:
        while len(running) < W and (ready_score and busy_pool < pool or ready_ingest):
            if ready_score and busy_pool < pool:
                heapq.heappush(running, (now + 4, "score", ready_score.pop(0))); busy_pool += 1
            else:
                heapq.heappush(running, (now + 1, "ingest", ready_ingest.pop(0)))
        now, kind, day = heapq.heappop(running)
        if kind == "ingest":
            ready_score.append(day)
        else:
            busy_pool -= 1
    return now

print(f"without a pool (10 concurrent scores possible): {makespan_with_pool(90, 10, 10):.0f} min")
print(f"with a pool of 3 for score: {makespan_with_pool(90, 10, 3):.0f} min (lower bound 90 x 4 / 3 = {90 * 4 / 3:.0f})")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
without a pool (10 concurrent scores possible): 45 min
with a pool of 3 for score: 121 min (lower bound 90 x 4 / 3 = 120)
```
:::
:::


Without a pool the backfill finishes sooner — but by opening up to ten
connections to a database that accepts three: in reality most `score` tasks
would fail and be retried, or overload a production system. With the pool,
the makespan is set by the bottleneck resource ($90 \cdot 4/3 = 120$ minutes,
a work bound like @prp-ops-greedy's with $W = 3$), and the remaining workers
run the ingests in the meantime.
:::

10:00, which interval does the most recent scheduled run process, and which
intervals would `catchup=True` create if the DAG had been paused since
2026-11-10? Why do pipelines process the *previous* day rather than the
current one?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
A daily run for the interval [2026-11-17 00:00, 2026-11-18 00:00) is
scheduled at the *end* of that interval, on 2026-11-18 at 00:00 — so on
2026-11-18 at 10:00 the latest scheduled run processes 2026-11-17. With
`catchup=True` after a pause since 2026-11-10, the scheduler creates one run
per missed interval, from the 10th to the 17th, each processing its own day
(which is why tasks must read their interval, @exr-ops8-airflow-easy). A day
is processed after it ends because its data are complete only then; processing
"today" would read a partial day and give a different answer at each re-run —
not deterministic in the sense of @prp-ops-backfill.
:::

::: {#exr-ops8-churn-retrain}
**Retraining and churn.** In @exr-ops8-retrain-medium, measure for each
retraining of the CUSUM policy the churn between the old and the new model on
the week's posts, and the share of the flips that are corrections
(wrong → right). Relate the numbers to @prp-ops-churn.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#a0a514f5 .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
model_ = ob.train_model(train.text, train.label)
ref = np.mean(model_.predict(weeks[0].text) == 0)
s_up = s_down = 0.0
for w in range(104):
    pred = model_.predict(weeks[w].text)
    share = np.mean(pred == 0)
    s_up, s_down = max(0, s_up + share - ref - 0.01), max(0, s_down - share + ref - 0.01)
    if max(s_up, s_down) > 0.06 and w >= 3:
        recent = pd.concat(weeks[w - 3: w + 1])
        new = ob.train_model(recent.text, recent.label)
        y = weeks[w].label.to_numpy(); p_old, p_new = pred, new.predict(weeks[w].text)
        churn = np.mean(p_old != p_new)
        fixes = np.sum((p_old != y) & (p_new == y)) / max(np.sum(p_old != p_new), 1)
        print(f"week {w:3d}: churn {churn:.3f}, accuracy {np.mean(p_old == y):.3f} -> {np.mean(p_new == y):.3f}, "
              f"share of flips that are corrections {fixes:.2f}")
        model_, ref, s_up, s_down = new, np.mean(p_new == 0), 0.0, 0.0
```

:::


Retrainings triggered by a real change flip several percent of the answers,
and most flips are corrections: the churn is close to its lower bound, the
accuracy gain (@eq-ops-churn-bounds). A retraining in a quiet period would
show the opposite profile — churn with no gain — which is the cost a schedule
pays for nothing.
:::
